lines.text: Why are cast-iron fire hydrants positioned every few hundred feet along American sidewalks?
What you see above ground is just the tip of an iceberg.
Beneath the pavement sits a massive dry barrel tube extending eight feet down into the earth.
In cold northern states, water is kept below the frost line to prevent freezing and bursting during freezing winters.
When firefighters crank open the top nut, a valve opens at the bottom, releasing pressurized water at thousands of gallons per minute.
Hydrants are color-coded: blue tops pump the highest flow over fifteen hundred gallons, while red pumps under five hundred.
That humble curb fixture provides instant life-saving firefighting power when every second counts.
